q: Who is the author of the chapter "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi"?
e: "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi" is an autobiographical narrative written by renowned fiction writer Mannu Bhandari.

q: Under which literary genre does "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi" fall?
e: Rather than a complete life history, Mannu Bhandari presents an autobiographical account of people and events that shaped her personality.

q: Where was Mannu Bhandari born?
e: Mannu Bhandari was born in 1931 in Bhanpura village of Mandsaur district, Madhya Pradesh.

q: In which city’s Brahmapuri locality do the author’s childhood memories begin?
e: Although born in Bhanpura, her memories begin at the two-storey house in Ajmer’s Brahmapuri locality.

q: Where did the author’s father live before moving to Ajmer?
e: Before coming to Ajmer, her father lived in Indore, where he enjoyed high prestige and prosperity.

q: What was the name of Mannu Bhandari’s elder sister?
e: Mannu Bhandari’s sister, two years older than her, was named Sushila, who was fair, healthy, and cheerful.

q: What did Mannu Bhandari’s father call the kitchen?
e: He called the kitchen "Bhatiyarkhana", believing that girls’ talent gets wasted inside it.

q: Who was the Hindi lecturer in college who inspired Mannu Bhandari’s literary and political awakening?
e: Sheela Agarwal, Hindi lecturer at Savitri Girls College, shaped Mannu Bhandari’s literary taste and political activism.

q: Which incomplete dictionary did the author’s father complete in Ajmer?
e: Her father completed his unfinished English-Hindi dictionary, which was the first of its kind.

q: Which complexion did the author’s father favour the most?
e: Her father strongly preferred a fair complexion, praising fair Sushila and comparing dark, frail Mannu to her.

q: In which year and at what age was elder sister Sushila married?
e: According to the text, in 1944 Sushila turned sixteen, got married, and moved to Kolkata.

q: Whose domain was the upper floor of the two-storey house in Ajmer?
e: In the two-storey house in Brahmapuri, the upper floor was her father’s domain filled with books and magazines.

q: Who was the father’s close friend who praised Mannu’s street speech to him?
e: Ajmer’s renowned physician and father’s intimate friend, Dr. Ambalal, wholeheartedly praised Mannu’s speech at the square.

q: What was Mannu Bhandari’s birth order among her five siblings?
e: Mannu Bhandari was the youngest of five siblings.

q: Which college did the author attend where Sheela Agarwal taught?
e: Mannu Bhandari studied at Savitri Girls College in Ajmer, where Sheela Agarwal taught Hindi.

q: What was the boundary for girls playing games in Ajmer during the author’s childhood?
o: The boundary walls of the home (neighbourhood houses)
e: At that time girls were not allowed out freely; the whole neighbourhood felt like home, yet games stayed within domestic boundaries.

q: Which games does Mannu Bhandari mention playing with her brothers?
o: Gilli-danda, kite flying, and grinding glass to coat kite-string (manja)
e: The author describes playing gilli-danda, flying kites, and preparing glass-coated manja with her brothers.

q: In which month and year was the college third year closed and Mannu along with a few girls barred from entering?
e: In May 1947, the college served notice to Sheela Agarwal, shut down the third-year classes, and barred Mannu and two or three others.

q: When were the closed third-year classes reopened at the college?
e: Following strong student protests and agitation, the third-year classes had to be reopened in August 1947.

q: In which year did Mannu Bhandari meet Sheela Agarwal?
e: In 1945, upon entering the first year of college, Mannu Bhandari came into contact with Hindi lecturer Sheela Agarwal.

q: With which quality of the earth did the author compare her mother?
e: The author writes that though her mother was uneducated, she possessed more patience and endurance than the earth itself.

q: What was the main cause behind the father’s financial downfall?
o: Betrayal by an intimate friend and resulting financial shocks
e: Betrayal by a trusted associate and severe financial setbacks in Indore forced him to relocate to Ajmer.

q: Which novel by Mannu Bhandari earned immense fame in Hindi literature?
e: "Aapka Bunty" and "Mahabhoj" are among Mannu Bhandari’s most acclaimed novels.

q: Whom did Mannu Bhandari’s father host and educate at his home in Indore?
e: During his Indore days, he was so generous that many students stayed at his home to study and later rose to high positions.

q: Why did the father initially flare up when a letter arrived from the college principal?
o: The college complained about Mannu’s indiscipline and leading student strikes
e: The principal wrote summoning him because girls walked out of classes at Mannu’s beckoning, which initially enraged him.

q: What did the father gain from compiling the English-Hindi dictionary?
o: Fame and prestige, though no financial profit
e: The dictionary brought him great renown and respect, yet yielded no financial returns.

q: Which games did Mannu Bhandari play with her female friends in childhood?
o: Langdi-taang, tag, kaali-tilo, and doll weddings
e: The author mentions playing langdi-taang, catch, kaali-tilo, and staging doll weddings with her friends.

q: What is the meaning of the word "Antarang"?
e: "Antarang" means intimate or very close; Dr. Ambalal was a close friend of her father.

q: To whom does Mannu Bhandari credit her initiation into serious literary reading and understanding?
e: Sheela Agarwal gave her curated books to read and held discussions that built her literary insight.

q: Which historic day did the author call the "greatest achievement of the century"?
e: She referred to India’s Independence on 15 August 1947 as the greatest achievement of the century.

q: What was the defining characteristic of Mannu Bhandari’s father’s temperament?
o: He was always calm and silent
He possessed contradictory traits: deeply tender and sensitive yet fiercely short-tempered and egoistic
He never spoke to his children
e: The author portrays him as full of contradictions—intensely compassionate on one hand, violently angry and egoistic on the other.

q: What negative change did betrayal bring into the father’s nature?
o: He donated everything and became a monk
He turned deeply suspicious of people around him
e: Betrayal by his own associates made him so distrustful that even his children occasionally bore the brunt of his suspicion.

q: Why could the author not regard her mother as her "ideal" (role model)?
o: Despite her sacrifice and patience, her helplessness and passive submission to every injustice were unacceptable to the author
Her mother did not love her
Her mother stopped her from studying
e: While the author felt deep sympathy for her mother, her silent submissiveness could never become her ideal.

q: Why did the mother always become the target of the father’s anger?
o: Mother silently endured every excess as her rightful lot without protesting
e: He vented his frustration over lost wealth and status on his wife because she endured everything silently.

q: Why did an inferiority complex take root inside Mannu during childhood?
o: Friends refused to talk to her
Father favoured fair skin and repeatedly compared dark, frail Mannu with fair, cheerful Sushila
Mother threw her out of the house
e: Constant praise for elder sister Sushila alongside disparaging comparisons instilled a deep inferiority complex in Mannu.

q: Why did Mannu’s father make her sit during political discussions at home?
o: He wanted her away from the kitchen so she would learn about national and world affairs and grow aware
e: Considering the kitchen a "bhatiyarkhana", he wanted Mannu to listen to political debates and develop awareness of the wider world.

q: Why did the father object when Mannu went onto the streets shouting slogans and leading strikes?
o: It clashed with his orthodox, patriarchal sense of honour to see a daughter shouting slogans on streets with boys
He feared she would drop out
e: He wanted awareness within four walls; marching and raising slogans with boys on the streets offended his conservative notions of propriety.

q: What turned the father’s anger into pride after meeting the college principal?
o: The principal gave Mannu a medal
The principal revealed Mannu’s extraordinary influence and leadership over all the girls at college
e: Hearing the principal acknowledge Mannu’s commanding influence over the students convinced him his daughter was truly exceptional, filling him with pride.

q: What did Dr. Ambalal tell the father regarding Mannu’s speech at the public square?
o: That Mannu should be locked inside
That he was amazed by her fiery speech and the father should come out and witness his daughter’s achievement
That the speech was too brief
e: Dr. Ambalal’s glowing praise of Mannu’s fiery oratory satisfied her father’s craving for social prestige and made him beam with pride.

q: How did Sheela Agarwal refine Mannu’s literary sensibility?
o: By making her memorize grammar only
By introducing works of Premchand, Sarat, Jainendra, Agyeya, and Yashpal and engaging her in deep discussions
e: Sheela Agarwal taught her not just to read books passively, but to critique, debate, and internalize literature.

q: When did Mannu first become the focus of her father’s special attention?
o: When elder brothers left for higher studies and after Sushila’s marriage in 1944 left the house quieter
e: Around age 14, after her brothers moved out and Sushila got married, her father finally noticed Mannu’s presence and potential.

q: Which two opposing tendencies reveal the father’s internal contradiction?
o: Modern aspiration (wanting his daughter educated and distinguished) versus patriarchal orthodoxy (objecting to public street activism)
Love for cricket and hate for music
e: He wanted his daughter to excel and gain renown, yet his conservative ego feared social judgment over her public independence.

q: What event related to the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) trials is mentioned in the chapter?
o: City-wide strike of schools, colleges, and shops, followed by students delivering speeches at Chaupar in the evening
e: In protest over the INA trials, Ajmer observed a strike and students gathered at Chaupar in the evening to deliver passionate speeches.

q: What evidence in the chapter demonstrates the father’s obsession with fame and social prestige?
o: He sat on stage every day
Hearing praise of his daughter from Dr. Ambalal and the principal instantly transformed his fury into pride
e: His primary weakness was his longing for public prestige; the moment he saw Mannu enhancing his standing, his anger melted into pride.

q: Why was Sheela Agarwal served a notice by the college authorities?
o: On charges of instigating female students and disrupting college discipline
e: The college management held Sheela Agarwal responsible for inspiring students to join protests and strikes.

q: What lasting effect of her childhood inferiority complex does the author note on her adult writing career?
o: Even today when she receives literary acclaim or honours, she finds it hard to believe and feels hesitant
She writes only about fair characters
e: Childhood comparisons left such a deep mark that even major literary accolades feel hard to believe.

q: How does the author describe the neighbourhood environment of her childhood in Ajmer?
o: A gated enclave of the rich
Warm and open, where every house in the neighbourhood felt like one’s own home
e: Contrasting it with modern apartment life, she recalls a warm community where the entire neighbourhood functioned like one family.

q: Whom does the author credit most significantly for shaping her personality and literary identity?
o: Her father and her lecturer Sheela Agarwal
e: She explicitly states that two individuals played the decisive role in shaping her personality: her father and Sheela Agarwal.

q: Which habit of her father persisted even during financial hardship?
o: His aristocratic habits, unfulfilled ambitions, and desire to stay at the top
e: Despite financial decline, he could not shed his Indore-era aristocratic habits and pride, deepening his frustration.

q: What do "Kaali-tilo" and "doll weddings" represent in the chapter?
o: Innocent domestic childhood games of girls and their restricted outdoor world
Secret codes of the freedom movement
e: These games depict both the innocence of childhood and the social restrictions placed on girls’ movement.

q: In Mannu Bhandari’s view, what distinguished the old neighbourhood from today’s "flat culture"?
o: Mutual warmth, shared trust, and open social bonding rather than isolated living
e: Unlike today’s isolated flat culture, the entire neighbourhood back then felt safe, intimate, and connected.

q: What role did Sheela Agarwal play in Mannu’s political involvement?
o: Advised her to stay away from politics
Beyond theory, debated national issues and inspired her to participate actively
e: While her father wanted political awareness confined indoors, Sheela Agarwal inspired Mannu to turn ideas into active participation.

q: What did Mannu Bhandari admire and what did she struggle with regarding her father?
o: She admired his sensitivity and love of learning, yet clashed with his anger, suspicion, and dominating ego
e: Her father nurtured her intellect, yet his temper, suspicion, and patriarchal dominance created lifelong friction.

q: What does the word "Dakiyanusi" mean as used in the chapter?
e: "Dakiyanusi" refers to outdated, orthodox, and rigid conservative thinking.

q: Why are the years "1946–47" pivotal in Mannu Bhandari’s life?
o: During those years she plunged actively into freedom struggle strikes, processions, and public speeches
e: The surging independence wave of 1946–47 broke her hesitation and transformed her into a fearless speaker and activist.

q: According to Mannu Bhandari, what resulted from her father’s pressure to "become exceptional"?
o: Even amidst inferiority feelings, it sparked an aspiration to achieve something meaningful and self-reliant
e: Her father’s high expectations combined with Sheela Agarwal’s mentorship spurred her to forge an independent identity.

q: Which personal victory did the author recall alongside the joy of India’s Independence?
o: The reopening of the shut third-year classes at her college and the students’ triumph
e: In August 1947, the students won their struggle to reopen the third year just as India achieved Independence on August 15.

q: What style of language is used in "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi"?
o: Natural, intimate, fluent Khadi Boli Hindi seamlessly blending common Urdu and English words
e: Mannu Bhandari writes in lucid, sensitive Hindi, naturally incorporating words like "wajood", "shiddat", "protective", and "complex".

q: What kind of national and social causes had the author’s father been associated with?
o: Congress activities, social reform, and promotion of education
e: In Indore, he had been active in Congress work as well as social reform and educational upliftment.

q: Which major discourse emerges prominently through "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi"?
o: Feminist discourse, women’s education, self-reliance, and struggle against patriarchal limits
e: Mannu carving an independent identity beyond her mother’s submissiveness and confronting patriarchal limits puts women’s empowerment at the heart of the text.

q: Context: Due to financial setbacks he moved to Ajmer and dedicated himself to finishing his English-Hindi dictionary. — What quality does this reflect?
o: Intellectual dedication, love of scholarship, and desire for honour despite adversity
e: Even after financial ruin, he pursued scholarly creation rather than giving up, valuing honour and intellect.

q: Comparing the mother’s life with Mannu’s, why did Mannu reject her mother’s model of endurance?
o: Because enduring injustice without protest erases self-respect and independent identity
Because mother wasn’t from a rich family
e: Mannu realized her mother’s sacrifice stemmed from helplessness and submission, whereas a self-respecting woman must claim her agency.

q: Based on the chapter, what can happen when parents repeatedly compare children’s skin colour or physical appearance?
o: It can implant a lifelong inferiority complex and self-doubt in the child’s psyche
e: Mannu herself exemplifies this: constant comparisons with fair Sushila left a lifelong sense of inadequacy despite later success.

q: Father kept Mannu away from the kitchen ("bhatiyarkhana") yet disliked her protesting in the streets. Which modern social attitude does this resemble?
o: Conditional modernity—encouraging girls’ education while still policing their public freedom and autonomy
e: Even today many families support education for daughters yet restrict their independent choices and public voice in the name of honour.

q: Context: Sheela Agarwal expanded her literary horizon and turned the indoor political awareness begun by her father into active participation. — What was Sheela Agarwal’s role?
o: She acted as a mentor who transformed passive awareness into active civic engagement and confidence
She taught her to hate her father
e: The father laid the intellectual foundation indoors, and Sheela Agarwal bridged thought with fearless real-world action.

q: What does the sudden shift in the father’s attitude after Dr. Ambalal’s praise illustrate?
o: His craving for prestige and pride outweighed his conservative reservations the moment society applauded his daughter
e: The very activism that angered him at home became a source of pride once a respected figure praised it publicly.

q: In childhood Mannu flew kites and prepared manja with her brothers—what aspect of her personality does this highlight?
o: From childhood she had a spirited tendency to step beyond passive gender stereotypes and join as an equal
e: Alongside traditional dolls, enjoying active games with brothers hinted early at her bold, energetic spirit.

q: What lesson do students draw from the shutting of third-year classes in May 1947 and their reopening in August 1947?
o: United, courageous, and principled student solidarity can overturn unjust administrative actions
e: Instead of bowing to intimidation, Mannu and her peers united and won back their rightful classes.

q: Where is Mannu Bhandari’s "quest for her own identity" most clearly reflected in the chapter?
o: Forging an independent literary and social identity distinct from both her mother’s submission and her father’s dominance
e: She absorbed her father’s intellectual spark while rejecting his patriarchal boundaries to chart her own path.

q: Listening to "political debates" over tea and snacks at home helped develop which skill in Mannu?
o: Critical thinking, socio-political awareness, and later the confidence for fiery public speaking
e: Childhood exposure to political debates planted the seeds of civic consciousness and articulate expression in her.

q: If Mannu Bhandari had not met a teacher like Sheela Agarwal, what would likely have been the impact on her life?
o: She would have become a doctor
She would become Mayor of Indore
Her literary talent and civic courage might have remained confined within domestic boundaries and family pressure
e: Sheela Agarwal turned her hesitation into conviction and connected her to great literature and public action.

q: What special meaning does the phrase "Yeh Bhi" (this too) convey in the title "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi"?
o: It is the only story in the world
It is copied from another author
Among many stories of her life, this is one vital story of how her writer-self was shaped
e: Though not a full autobiography, it presents "this story too"—the formative narrative of how her writing persona emerged.

q: Context: Only after siblings left home did her father’s attention focus on Mannu. — What family reality does this highlight?
o: In large families, the youngest girl—especially if deemed less striking—often goes unnoticed until elders leave
e: Being the youngest and dusky among five siblings, Mannu remained largely in the background until her brothers left and Sushila married.

q: Why did contrasting qualities like "fire" and "flower" coexist in her father’s personality?
o: Naturally kind and generous, betrayal, financial ruin, and wounded ego turned him short-tempered and suspicious
e: Life’s betrayals and economic fall layered bitterness, suspicion, and rage over his originally tender nature.

q: “The frustration of a person broken by financial setbacks often vents itself on family” — Which part of the chapter reflects this?
o: Father venting his frustration over lost wealth and prestige onto his silent wife
e: Inability to maintain former grandeur amid financial decline bred frustration that he directed at his uncomplaining wife.

q: Participation in the freedom movement helped Mannu overcome which personal struggle?
e: Delivering public speeches and leading peers helped her discover her inner strength and break past childhood hesitation.

q: Why does Mannu Bhandari appear both "grateful and critical" rather than hostile toward her father?
o: Because she acknowledges he gave her intellectual grounding and ambition, even while honestly critiquing his temper and orthodoxy
Because she wanted money from him
e: As an honest memoirist, she offers a balanced assessment—acknowledging both his inspiring role and his hurtful flaws.

q: Why did the father not punish Mannu even after the college principal complained against her?
o: Along with complaining, the principal admitted Mannu’s extraordinary leadership and influence over the entire college
e: The principal’s admission proved Mannu was a leader rather than a follower, appealing directly to his pride in raising someone extraordinary.

q: What key example of "self-reliance" and "women’s empowerment" emerges from Mannu Bhandari’s life in the chapter?
o: Developing literary discernment, raising her voice for rights in public life, and building an independent identity
e: Refusing to remain confined by patriarchal norms, she empowered herself through literature, critical thought, and public activism.

q: Why are "Sarat, Premchand, Jainendra, Agyeya, and Yashpal" mentioned in "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi"?
o: They were principals at Ajmer college
To highlight the acclaimed writers Sheela Agarwal introduced to Mannu, which shaped her literary sensibility
e: Reading these great realist and psychological writers trained Mannu to examine human relationships and society deeply.

q: Why is the "English-Hindi dictionary" compiled by her father in Ajmer given importance in the text?
o: It was the first of its kind, bringing him fame and prestige without financial relief, deepening his inner frustration
It made the family rich overnight
It was confiscated by the British
e: The dictionary symbolizes his intellectual labour and quest for prestige, though its lack of income sustained his financial anxiety.

q: How does the author portray young women’s participation in the "1946–47 period"?
o: Even students of Savitri Girls College stepped forward fearlessly into morning rallies, strikes, and processions
They had no concern for college
e: During that wave of the freedom struggle, young women broke social taboos to march and protest alongside everyone else.

q: Context: "Though uneducated, Mother had more patience and endurance than the earth." — Why is "earth" used as the comparison here?
o: Because the house was made of mud
Because just as the earth silently bears everything and keeps giving, her mother endured all and gave unconditionally
Because mother slept on the floor
e: Earth is the timeless emblem of forbearance and selfless giving, matching the mother’s silent endurance.

q: What attitude toward kitchen work did the father express by calling it "Bhatiyarkhana"?
o: Food tastes good in the kitchen
Spending all day in the kitchen wastes a woman’s intellectual potential and talent
e: He did not want his daughter reduced solely to domestic cooking, wishing instead for her intellectual growth.

q: When her father turned suspicious amid adversity, who suffered most from this trait according to the text?
o: His own family—especially his wife and children—who bore his unprovoked anger and suspicion
e: His suspicion and sudden rages strained family harmony, directly hurting his wife and children.

q: Whose influence does the author acknowledge having absorbed even unconsciously into her personality?
o: Her father’s traits and complexities, which entered her subconsciously despite her disagreements with him
e: She candidly admits that despite clashing with him, many of her father’s strengths and flaws seeped into her subconsciously.

q: If a student today faces an unfair notice on a social or academic issue, what inspiration does "Ek Kahani Yeh Bhi" offer?
o: Stand firm on righteous issues with reason, unity, and fearlessness
e: Mannu and her classmates did not surrender when third-year classes were shut; their united stand won them back.

q: “Participating in the freedom struggle was not solely men’s domain” — How is this proved in the chapter?
o: Through Mannu Bhandari and fellow college girls leading strikes, marches, slogans, and public speeches
e: Active participation by Mannu and her female peers proved that young women played a vibrant part in the independence movement.

q: What long-term effect did Sheela Agarwal’s habit of holding debates on literary texts likely have on Mannu’s writing?
o: It nurtured independent critical judgment and deep insight into human psychology, visible in her later stories
She got a bad habit of arguing
e: Debating literature cultivated critical thinking and psychological depth that enriched her renowned fiction.

q: With what sentiment does the author contrast her childhood "four walls of the neighbourhood" with modern times?
o: Nostalgia for old warmth and concern over modern urban isolation
e: She notes that despite mobility limits back then, the warmth of shared community far surpassed today’s alienated flat living.
